text: You've been filtering and transforming trip data for two lessons now. This lesson puts it to work answering real questions: aggregating by group, and joining in a second table so numeric IDs become real, readable place names.

This is exactly pandas' groupby and agg from Lesson 24, just now running over a dataset with millions of real trip records that pandas alone would struggle with. alias matters here specifically — without it, Spark would name the result something clunky like avg of fare_amount, which is awkward to reference later.

You can group by more than one column at once, exactly like the pandas version — each unique combination of vendor and passenger count becomes its own group. orderBy is the sort step, and it's applied after the aggregation so the result reads sensibly top to bottom.

A raw trip record only has a numeric pickup location ID, which isn't useful in a report anyone would actually read. Joining to the real taxi zone lookup table turns that ID into an actual Zone and Borough name. The left join keeps every trip even on the rare chance a location ID has no match.

This chains together everything the chapter's built so far: join first to get readable zone names, filter out bad fares, then aggregate. That's also exactly the shape the mini capstone's pipeline is going to take in the next two lessons.

Once you can explain why you'd join to the zone lookup table before grouping by zone name, rather than after, you're ready for Lesson 47 — where we pull everything from the last three chapters together into one real, complete pipeline.
